title: GMOs and Genetic Engineering
hook: By deliberately rewriting an organism's DNA, scientists can make bacteria brew human insulin or crops resist pests — traits nature never handed them.
key_points: Genetic engineering means directly altering an organism's DNA to give it new traits.
A GMO is any organism whose genome has been changed using these lab techniques.
Genes can be moved between species — even from a bacterium into a plant.
Real-world uses include insulin-producing microbes, pest-resistant crops, and vitamin-enriched rice.
It differs from old-fashioned breeding by being faster, more precise, and not limited to one species.
content_html: Genetic engineering is the deliberate rewriting of an organism's DNA to give it traits it never had. An organism changed this way is called a genetically modified organism, or GMO. Because the genetic code is universal, a gene from one species can work inside another — which is how bacteria were taught to brew human insulin and how some crops carry built-in pest resistance.
extra_html: The toolkit ranges from cutting and pasting individual genes to precise editors like CRISPR. Scientists isolate a gene that codes for a useful trait, insert it into a target organism's genome, and let the cell read it like any of its own instructions. As Encyclopaedia Britannica describes, applications now span medicine (insulin, vaccines, clotting factors), agriculture (insect-resistant and vitamin-enriched crops), and research. The same power fuels ongoing debate about safety, labeling, and ecological effects — questions of governance more than of whether the science works.

related.title: CRISPR: Molecular Scissors for DNA
related.hook: Borrowed from a bacterial immune system, CRISPR lets scientists find a precise spot in the genome and cut it — turning gene editing into something almost routine.

related.title: How Genes Become Traits
related.hook: You inherit two copies of every gene — one from each parent — and the way those copies interact helps decide everything from eye color to blood type.

related.title: What Is DNA?
related.hook: A four-letter chemical code, coiled into a double helix, carries the full instruction manual for building and running a living thing.

flashcards.back_html: A genetically modified organism — one whose DNA has been deliberately altered in the lab to give it new traits, rather than through ordinary breeding.

flashcards.prompt: Which is a real example of genetic engineering at work?

choices.text: Bacteria engineered to produce human insulin
A dog trained to fetch the newspaper
A plant grown in richer soil

flashcards.explanation_html: Inserting the human insulin gene into bacteria lets them manufacture the hormone in vats — a foundational triumph of genetic engineering.

flashcards.prompt: How does genetic engineering differ from traditional breeding?

choices.text: It can move a gene between unrelated species and targets DNA directly
It only works on animals, never plants
It changes traits without touching the DNA at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Breeding shuffles genes within compatible species over generations; engineering can transfer a single chosen gene across the tree of life in one step.
